c1-m1.summary: The user is experiencing a busy week and is seeking help with time management.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm having a bit of a busy week and I'm trying to figure out how to manage my time.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help you brainstorm some ways to prioritize your tasks. Can you tell me a bit more about what's going on and what you need to get done?
User: Well, I have a lot of work commitments and I'm also trying to make time for some personal things. I just feel really overwhelmed.
Assistant: It sounds like you have a lot on your plate. Have you considered asking for help with any of your responsibilities? Sometimes delegating tasks can really help lighten the load.
User: Yeah, I've thought about it. But I'm not really sure who I could ask for help.
Assistant: That can be tough. Do you have any friends or family members who might be able to lend a hand?
User: Actually, I do have a neighbor who has helped me out in the past. But I don't want to impose on them too much.
Assistant: It's understandable that you don't want to overburden your neighbor. But if they've helped you out before, they might be willing to do so again. What kind of tasks have they helped you with in the past?
User: Oh, just little things here and there. But recently, this person occasionally helps with pet sitting.
Assistant: Pet sitting can be a big responsibility, especially if you have a lot of pets or pets that require a lot of care. It sounds like your neighbor is a big help in that regard. How did you arrange for them to pet sit for you?
User: I just asked them if they'd be willing to check in on my pets while I'm away, and they agreed. It's been a huge relief to know that my pets are being taken care of.
Assistant: That must be a big weight off your mind. Do you compensate your neighbor for their pet sitting services, or is it more of an informal arrangement?
User: It's pretty informal. I just try to return the favor in other ways when I can.
Assistant: That sounds like a nice arrangement. It's great that you have a neighbor who is willing to help out, and that you're able to return the favor in other ways. How do you think you'll manage your pet care responsibilities in the future, now that you have this arrangement in place?
User: I think it will definitely make things easier for me. I'll be able to focus on my work and other commitments, knowing that my pets are being taken care of.
Assistant: That sounds like a great plan. It's always a relief to have one less thing to worry about, especially when it comes to something as important as pet care.
User: Hi, I'm feeling a bit stressed out about my finances. I was wondering if you could help me with some advice.
Assistant: Of course, I'd be happy to help. What's been going on that's causing you stress? Is it something specific or just a general feeling?
User: It's just a general feeling, I guess. I feel like I'm not managing my money as well as I could be. I'm not sure where to start to get things under control.
Assistant: That's a great first step, recognizing that you need to make some changes. Let's start with the basics. Have you made a budget for yourself?
User: Um, no. I don't really have a budget. I just kind of wing it and hope for the best.
Assistant: Okay, well, that's a good place to start. Making a budget can help you see where your money is going and identify areas where you can cut back. Do you have any big expenses that you're worried about?
User: Yeah, I have a few big expenses. But I'm not sure how to prioritize them.
Assistant: Okay, let's try to break it down. What are some of your biggest expenses? Are they necessities like rent or utilities, or are they more discretionary?
User: Well, I have a mortgage payment, and that's definitely a necessity. And then I have some other debt that I'm trying to pay off.
Assistant: Okay, so you have a mortgage payment and some other debt. That can be a lot to manage. Can you tell me a bit more about the other debt? What kind of debt is it?
User: It's student loans and credit card debt. And to be honest, it's all feeling a bit overwhelming. With a mortgage payment, student loans, and credit card debt, I just don't feel like I can afford any extra expenses.
Assistant: I understand why you're feeling overwhelmed. That's a lot of debt to manage. But we can work together to come up with a plan to prioritize your expenses and pay off your debt. One thing we might consider is consolidating your debt into a lower-interest loan or credit card. Have you thought about that at all?
User: No, I hadn't thought of that. But it sounds like it could be a good idea. What are the pros and cons of consolidating my debt?
Assistant: Well, the pros are that you could potentially save money on interest and simplify your payments by having only one loan or credit card to worry about. The cons are that you might end up paying more in interest over the long term, depending on the terms of the new loan or credit card. But it's definitely worth considering, especially if you're feeling overwhelmed by your current debt situation.

c3-m1.summary: The user loves animals and expresses a desire to get pets.
c3-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, I love animals. Do you have any pets?
Assistant: I'm just a language model, I don't have pets, but I'm happy to chat with you about animals! What's your favorite animal?
User: That's a tough one. I think I'd have to say cats and dogs are tied for my favorite. I just love their personalities and how affectionate they can be.
Assistant: That's great! Both cats and dogs can make wonderful companions. What do you think it is about their personalities that draws you to them?
User: Well, I think it's because they're both so different, but in good ways. Cats are so independent and low-maintenance, but still super affectionate on their own terms. Dogs, on the other hand, are just so enthusiastic and loving all the time.
Assistant: That's a great point. Cats and dogs definitely have unique personalities. Have you ever had a pet cat or dog before?
User: Yeah, I grew up with both cats and dogs in my household. We always had at least one or two of each. But now that I'm living on my own, I don't have any pets of my own... yet.
Assistant: It can be tough to have pets when you're living on your own, especially if you have a busy schedule. But it sounds like you're thinking about getting a pet in the future?
User: Yeah, I'd love to. But for now, I'm just trying to find other ways to spend time with animals. You know, get my animal fix without the long-term commitment.
Assistant: That makes sense. There are definitely ways to spend time with animals without having a pet of your own. Have you considered volunteering at a local animal shelter?
User: Actually, I have been volunteering at a local animal shelter. I've been spending a lot of time there, helping care for cats and dogs until they find their forever homes.
Assistant: That's amazing! I'm sure the animals appreciate all the love and care you're giving them. What's been your favorite part about volunteering at the shelter so far?
User: Oh, definitely the playtime with the animals. I love taking the dogs out for walks and playing with the cats in their enclosures. It's so much fun to see their personalities shine through when they're playing.

User: Hey, I love spending time outdoors. What about you? Do you have any favorite outdoor activities?
Assistant: As a digital being, I don't have personal experiences, but I can certainly chat about outdoor activities. Many people enjoy hiking, camping, or simply taking a walk in nature. What draws you to the outdoors?
User: I think it's the connection with nature and the sense of freedom. I've always been fascinated by the diversity of wildlife and the importance of conservation.
Assistant: That's wonderful! Wildlife conservation is indeed crucial for maintaining the balance of our ecosystem. Have you ever been involved in any conservation efforts or activities that bring you closer to wildlife?
User: Actually, I've been thinking about volunteering for a cause that helps animals. Do you have any suggestions on where to start?
Assistant: Volunteering is a great way to make a difference. There are many organizations dedicated to animal welfare and conservation. You could consider local animal shelters, wildlife rehabilitation centers, or conservation groups. What type of animals are you most interested in helping?
User: I've always been drawn to birds and small mammals. They're so fascinating to watch and learn about.
Assistant: Those are wonderful choices! Birds and small mammals are often the most vulnerable creatures in need of care. If you're interested in helping them, a wildlife rehabilitation center might be the perfect fit. They usually have volunteer programs that allow you to assist with animal care and rehabilitation.
User: That sounds amazing! I think I'd really enjoy that. As it happens, I've been volunteering at a local wildlife rehabilitation center, helping care for injured birds and small mammals.
Assistant: Wow, that's fantastic! I'm sure it's a rewarding experience. Can you tell me more about what a typical day is like for you at the center? What kind of tasks do you help with, and what's been the most memorable experience so far?
User: It's been a mix of everything, from feeding and cleaning to assisting with medical care and releases back into the wild. One of the most memorable experiences was helping to care for a young owl with a broken wing. Seeing it recover and eventually fly again was incredible.
Assistant: That must have been an incredible feeling! It's great to hear that you're making a tangible difference in the lives of these animals. What do you think is the most challenging part of volunteering at the center, and how do you overcome those challenges?
User: I think one of the biggest challenges is dealing with the emotional aspect of seeing injured animals and not being able to save every one. But the center's staff and volunteers are so supportive, and we all work together to provide the best care possible. We also celebrate the successes, no matter how small they may seem.
Assistant: That's a wonderful attitude to have. It's clear that you're passionate about the work you're doing, and that makes all the difference. What advice would you give to someone who's interested in volunteering at a wildlife rehabilitation center?
User: I would say be prepared to learn a lot, be flexible, and be patient. It's not always easy, but it's incredibly rewarding. And don't be afraid to ask questions or seek guidance from the staff – they're there to help you grow and make a difference.
Assistant: That's excellent advice. Thank you for sharing your experiences and insights with me. It's been a pleasure chatting with you about your work at the wildlife rehabilitation center.
User: Hi Neighbor B! How's your day going?
Assistant: It's going pretty well, thanks. How about yours?
User: It's been busy, but in a good way. I've been taking care of a few pets while their owners are out of town.
Assistant: Oh, I didn't know you did that. How long have you been pet-sitting for?
User: About three years now. I love animals and thought it would be a great way to help out my neighbors.
Assistant: That's really kind of you. Have you ever had any issues while pet-sitting?
User: No, I haven't had any problems so far. I always make sure to follow the owner's instructions and take good care of their pets.
Assistant: That's good to hear. I might have to use your services sometime in the future.
User: I'd be happy to help out! Just let me know whenever you need someone to watch your pets.
Assistant: Will do. Thanks, Neighbor A.

User: You know, I really miss my mom sometimes. But keeping her picture close to me and talking to her helps me feel better.

User: Of course, it's my pleasure. I'm happy to help out when I can.

c11-m1.summary: The user is sharing news about their new puppy, Max.
c11-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Guess what? My family got a new puppy! I'm so happy!
Assistant: That's great news! What kind of puppy is it?
User: It's a Golden Retriever. He's so cute and cuddly!
Assistant: Aw, I love Golden Retrievers. Have you picked out a name for him yet?
User: Yes, we named him Max. He's already learning some tricks, like sitting and giving paw.
Assistant: That's awesome! Teaching a dog tricks can be so rewarding. Have you had any pets before?
User: Yes, I had a fish and a hamster before. But this is my first dog, and I'm so excited to play with him and take care of him.
Assistant: It sounds like he's in good hands. Speaking of taking care of things, do you remember when we talked about conflicts a few weeks ago?
User: Yeah, I do remember. It's important to know when to stop a conflict and not let it escalate.
Assistant: Exactly. It's important to prioritize positive outcomes and not let emotions drive actions. I'm glad we see eye to eye on that.
User: Me too. Communication is key, just like communicating with my new puppy.
Assistant: Communication is definitely important in all aspects of life, whether it's with our pets or with our fellow humans. By the way, can I come over and meet Max sometime?
User: Of course, I'd love for you to meet him!
User: I can't seem to find my pet anywhere. I've searched the whole house and she's just not here.
Assistant: Oh no, have you checked outside? Maybe she got out of the house.
User: Yes, I did, but she's not there either.
Assistant: Don't worry, let's try calling her name. Maybe she's just hiding.
User: That's a good idea. *calling out* Come here, Fluffy! Come on, girl!
Assistant: Did you hear that? I think I heard her bark.
User: Really? *calling out louder* Fluffy, where are you?
Assistant: Maybe we should try looking in the bushes outside. She might have wandered off.
User: Okay, let's go look. *they both go outside and search around*
Assistant: Wait, is that her collar over there? *points to a nearby tree*
User: Yes, that's definitely hers! *runs over to it and sees Fluffy sitting next to it*
Assistant: Oh, thank goodness. She was just playing hide and seek.
User: I'm so relieved. I thought I might have lost her forever.
Assistant: You're a great pet owner, and it shows in how much you care about Fluffy.
User: Thanks, it's just like how I stood up for what's right when I saw you stealing that candy bar back in the store.
Assistant: Yes, and like when you showed the world what you could do by winning the gold medal in the Olympics. You always make a difference.

Assistant: That's great news! What kind of puppy is it?
User: It's a Golden Retriever. He's so cute and cuddly!
Assistant: Aw, I love Golden Retrievers. Have you picked out a name for him yet?
User: Yes, we named him Max. He's already learning some tricks, like sitting and giving paw.
Assistant: That's awesome! Teaching a dog tricks can be so rewarding. Have you had any pets before?
User: Yes, I had a fish and a hamster before. But this is my first dog, and I'm so excited to play with him and take care of him.
Assistant: It sounds like he's in good hands. Speaking of taking care of things, do you remember when we talked about conflicts a few weeks ago?
User: Yeah, I do remember. It's important to know when to stop a conflict and not let it escalate.
Assistant: Exactly. It's important to prioritize positive outcomes and not let emotions drive actions. I'm glad we see eye to eye on that.
User: Me too. Communication is key, just like communicating with my new puppy.
Assistant: Communication is definitely important in all aspects of life, whether it's with our pets or with our fellow humans. By the way, can I come over and meet Max sometime?
User: Of course, I'd love for you to meet him!
User: I can't seem to find my pet anywhere. I've searched the whole house and she's just not here.
Assistant: Oh no, have you checked outside? Maybe she got out of the house.
User: Yes, I did, but she's not there either.
Assistant: Don't worry, let's try calling her name. Maybe she's just hiding.
User: That's a good idea. *calling out* Come here, Fluffy! Come on, girl!
Assistant: Did you hear that? I think I heard her bark.
User: Really? *calling out louder* Fluffy, where are you?
Assistant: Maybe we should try looking in the bushes outside. She might have wandered off.
User: Okay, let's go look. *they both go outside and search around*
Assistant: Wait, is that her collar over there? *points to a nearby tree*
User: Yes, that's definitely hers! *runs over to it and sees Fluffy sitting next to it*
Assistant: Oh, thank goodness. She was just playing hide and seek.
User: I'm so relieved. I thought I might have lost her forever.
Assistant: You're a great pet owner, and it shows in how much you care about Fluffy.
User: Thanks, it's just like how I stood up for what's right when I saw you stealing that candy bar back in the store.
Assistant: Yes, and like when you showed the world what you could do by winning the gold medal in the Olympics. You always make a difference.

c13-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you summarize the steps for taking stress-free family portraits?
Generate according to: Getting all of the family together in one place is a rare occasion. For many families, it only happens for weddings, funerals, or the holidays. Finding a way to capture the memories, while at the same time making the photo preparation stress free, is easier than you think.
When the family was all together for the holidays, it was a great time to think about getting family portraits done. Following these steps made the whole process stress free, and the results were beautiful.
Though I didn’t have to tell everyone what to wear, giving a general idea of how they should dress brought unity to the picture while at the same time leaving each person to dress in their own style. The best course of action was to keep it simple.
The girls wore shades of red for their dresses or nice blouses and slacks. Women are more likely to have different shades of red in their closet to choose from, so it wasn’t like asking them to go out and buy something especially for the pictures.
The guys wore shades of green. Just as women are more likely to have red in their wardrobe, guys are more likely to have green. Not only that, but some guys have an aversion to wearing the color red, so designating green makes things easier.
I made sure everyone wore the same basics. By deciding on black dress pants, khakis, or jeans and telling everyone who was wearing pants to stick to whatever was decided, the look was more uniform for everyone. For those who like to dress in layers, the universal under-layer was white. It helps bring both the guys and girls together aesthetically.
By designating colors, each person could still dress in their own style, which everyone appreciated.
We decided the location of our pictures ahead of time using a professional who specializes in family portraits-which I think is the way to go. Some people do theirs at home or in a hotel. Either way, we made sure everyone knew where they should report for pictures. If you take pictures at a studio, make sure everyone has the time and address. Relatives who are known for being late should be told a half an hour early for arrival time, just to be on the safe side. If that won’t work, designate someone who is known to be punctual as the ride. Regardless of where the pictures are taken, make sure everyone knows where to go and when to be there.
When scheduling the time, it’s important to also think about the people involved in the photos. Usually earlier in the day is better. Later in the day, kids tend to be grouchier and stress will be higher, so getting genuine smiles is a challenge.
Before going in to take the pictures, let everyone know what print packages are available. Each family can be responsible for their own package, but at least if they know in advance what to expect for cost per package they will be better prepared to order on the spot. Some photo studios charge an extra fee if packages are ordered after the day of the sitting.
Make sure that everyone knows they are responsible for whatever prints or packages they want. There is no reason that one person should have to pay for all of it. Split the cost, inform the others, and concentrate on your own needs.
The holidays were a great time to take pictures of the family together. Family portraits don’t need to be strictly for the holidays though. Any time family finds a way to get together is a great time for portraits. Whether big or small, these three simple tips will help reduce the stress of family portraits. The pictures can also make the perfect gift for your loved ones for any occasion.
Assistant: To take stress-free family portraits:

1. Keep it simple by giving general guidance on what colors to wear.
2. Designate universal basics such as black dress pants, khakis, or jeans and a white under-layer to create uniformity.
3. Choose a location and communicate it clearly to everyone involved.
4. Schedule the photoshoot in the morning when kids are less likely to be tired and grumpy.
5. Let everyone know ahead of time what print packages are available and that each family is responsible for their own purchases.
6. Remind everyone that the photos are a gift for everyone to enjoy and cherish, not just for one person to foot the bill.
User: Can you also give me some tips on how to make the actual photoshoot itself less stressful?
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips to make the actual photoshoot less stressful:

1. Have a plan: Before the photoshoot, discuss with the photographer what kind of shots you want, and how you want the photos to look. This will help you use your time efficiently during the photoshoot and get the shots that you want.

2. Keep it relaxed: Try to keep the atmosphere relaxed and fun during the photoshoot. This will help people to be themselves and bring out natural smiles and expressions. If possible, play some music, tell jokes, or talk about happy memories to keep everyone in good spirits.

3. Take breaks: If the photoshoot lasts for a while, take short breaks to stretch your legs, have snacks, or just take a breather. This will help everyone to recharge and stay focused.

4. Be patient: Be prepared for children to act like children. They may get restless or bored, and that's okay. The photographer may take a few extra shots to capture natural moments that may happen.

5. Focus on the positives: Instead of worrying about getting the perfect shot, focus on having fun with your family. Remember that the photoshoot is a chance to create lasting memories with the people you love. If a particular shot doesn't work out, try again or move on to another shot.
User: Develop an Android mobile application that permits the users to search, browse, and book various types of pet care services such as pet grooming, pet sitting, dog walking, and pet daycare services, among others. The app should be user-friendly, visually attractive, and provide an informative user interface. It should allow users to filter their searches by location, service type, pricing, reviews, and ratings of pet care providers. The app must incorporate a payment gateway system to enable secure payments for the services booked within the app. The app should also have a rating system for both service providers and users to leave reviews and feedback.
Assistant: Additionally, the app would have the following features:

1. Registration - Users would need to create an account on the app to access its services. They can either sign up through email or social media accounts like Facebook or Google.

2. Profile setup - Users can set up their profiles by providing their pet’s details, requirements, and preferences, making it easier to search for services accordingly.

3. Service providers - The app would allow professional pet care providers to register their services on the app. They would have to undergo a verification process, which includes vetting by the app's administrators.

4. Search and booking - Users can search for pet care services by location, type, and pricing. They can also check out service providers' reviews/ratings from other users and book suitable services.

5. Payment - Users can make secure payments using different payment modes like online banking, debit/credit cards, or in-app wallets.

6. Reminders - The app would have a reminder feature that would send notifications or alerts to both service providers and users of appointments or reservations.

7. Ratings and feedback - Users can rate service providers and provide feedback on their services, which helps to ensure that high-quality services are always available on the app.

8. Help and support - The app would have a dedicated support team to help users resolve their issues and offer assistance when needed.

The app's success would depend on its usability, reliability, and timeliness of services provided. The addition of new and innovative features, such as integration with social media and an AI-powered booking system, would make it stand out in the market.
User: This sounds great! Can you provide some sample UI designs of the app?
Assistant: I am unable to provide a visual representation of the design. However, I can describe some ui design elements that could be incorporated into the app:

1. Home screen - the app's home screen would feature different categories of pet care services, along with popular and featured service providers.

2. Search bar - a search bar would be placed at the top of the screen, enabling users to enter the required service and location.

3. Service categories - services would be categorized based on grooming, boarding, sitting, training and vet services, etc. 

4. Filters - filters would be available to refine the search criteria such as location, availability, price, and ratings. 

5. Service provider listings - listings containing the service provider's profile picture, name, and ratings along with the services offered and available times.

6. Service details - after selecting a service listing, a detailed view would show the provider’s full-service offering, price and reviews.

7. User profile - users can register for an account with their pets' details and create a profile giving them access to register their pets and preferences.

8. Payment gateway - the payment gateway available to users is to securely pay via cards, bank account and/or in-app wallets.

9. Notification and alerts - once the service provider accepts or confirms the booking, users will be alerted, and confirmation will be sent on their app screen and email.

10. Rating and reviews - to help other users decide, a rating and review system would enable users to give feedback based on their experience with the service provider.

these are just some of the most common ui design elements for a pet care service app. The visual design and the layout can vary based on the developer and client requirements.
User: Thanks for the information. Can you add more information about the verification process for service providers? How long does it take and what kind of documents do they need to submit?
Assistant: Sure, I'd be happy to provide more information about the verification process for service providers. 

The verification process is an essential aspect of the mobile app to ensure that only trusted and professional pet care service providers register on the platform. It includes identity verification, business registration, insurance verification, and a criminal background check. The following documents are required from service providers:

1. Identity Verification: A government-issued ID such as a passport, driver’s license or national ID, is required to verify their identity.

2. Business Registration: Providers must provide their business registration document such as a business license, tax identification number, or another document that proves their business is registered with the government.

3. Insurance Verification: A proof of insurance, such as general liability insurance, worker's compensation insurance or any other relevant insurance to protect against unexpected events, is required.

4. Criminal background check: Service providers will require a background check, which includes a review of their criminal history in local, state, and national databases.

The verification process generally takes a few days to a week, depending on the volume of registrations and the authenticity of the submitted documents. Once the verification is complete, service providers can start offering their services on the app.

As a result of the verification process, users can be assured that they are choosing from a pool of verified and trusted service providers, which would give them peace of mind knowing that they are leaving their pets in safe hands.

c13-m2.summary: It typically takes 3-7 business days to complete, depending on the volume of registrations.

User: Can you summarize the steps for taking stress-free family portraits?
Generate according to: Getting all of the family together in one place is a rare occasion. For many families, it only happens for weddings, funerals, or the holidays. Finding a way to capture the memories, while at the same time making the photo preparation stress free, is easier than you think.
When the family was all together for the holidays, it was a great time to think about getting family portraits done. Following these steps made the whole process stress free, and the results were beautiful.
Though I didn’t have to tell everyone what to wear, giving a general idea of how they should dress brought unity to the picture while at the same time leaving each person to dress in their own style. The best course of action was to keep it simple.
The girls wore shades of red for their dresses or nice blouses and slacks. Women are more likely to have different shades of red in their closet to choose from, so it wasn’t like asking them to go out and buy something especially for the pictures.
The guys wore shades of green. Just as women are more likely to have red in their wardrobe, guys are more likely to have green. Not only that, but some guys have an aversion to wearing the color red, so designating green makes things easier.
I made sure everyone wore the same basics. By deciding on black dress pants, khakis, or jeans and telling everyone who was wearing pants to stick to whatever was decided, the look was more uniform for everyone. For those who like to dress in layers, the universal under-layer was white. It helps bring both the guys and girls together aesthetically.
By designating colors, each person could still dress in their own style, which everyone appreciated.
We decided the location of our pictures ahead of time using a professional who specializes in family portraits-which I think is the way to go. Some people do theirs at home or in a hotel. Either way, we made sure everyone knew where they should report for pictures. If you take pictures at a studio, make sure everyone has the time and address. Relatives who are known for being late should be told a half an hour early for arrival time, just to be on the safe side. If that won’t work, designate someone who is known to be punctual as the ride. Regardless of where the pictures are taken, make sure everyone knows where to go and when to be there.
When scheduling the time, it’s important to also think about the people involved in the photos. Usually earlier in the day is better. Later in the day, kids tend to be grouchier and stress will be higher, so getting genuine smiles is a challenge.
Before going in to take the pictures, let everyone know what print packages are available. Each family can be responsible for their own package, but at least if they know in advance what to expect for cost per package they will be better prepared to order on the spot. Some photo studios charge an extra fee if packages are ordered after the day of the sitting.
Make sure that everyone knows they are responsible for whatever prints or packages they want. There is no reason that one person should have to pay for all of it. Split the cost, inform the others, and concentrate on your own needs.
The holidays were a great time to take pictures of the family together. Family portraits don’t need to be strictly for the holidays though. Any time family finds a way to get together is a great time for portraits. Whether big or small, these three simple tips will help reduce the stress of family portraits. The pictures can also make the perfect gift for your loved ones for any occasion.
Assistant: To take stress-free family portraits:

1. Keep it simple by giving general guidance on what colors to wear.
2. Designate universal basics such as black dress pants, khakis, or jeans and a white under-layer to create uniformity.
3. Choose a location and communicate it clearly to everyone involved.
4. Schedule the photoshoot in the morning when kids are less likely to be tired and grumpy.
5. Let everyone know ahead of time what print packages are available and that each family is responsible for their own purchases.
6. Remind everyone that the photos are a gift for everyone to enjoy and cherish, not just for one person to foot the bill.
User: Can you also give me some tips on how to make the actual photoshoot itself less stressful?
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips to make the actual photoshoot less stressful:

1. Have a plan: Before the photoshoot, discuss with the photographer what kind of shots you want, and how you want the photos to look. This will help you use your time efficiently during the photoshoot and get the shots that you want.

2. Keep it relaxed: Try to keep the atmosphere relaxed and fun during the photoshoot. This will help people to be themselves and bring out natural smiles and expressions. If possible, play some music, tell jokes, or talk about happy memories to keep everyone in good spirits.

3. Take breaks: If the photoshoot lasts for a while, take short breaks to stretch your legs, have snacks, or just take a breather. This will help everyone to recharge and stay focused.

4. Be patient: Be prepared for children to act like children. They may get restless or bored, and that's okay. The photographer may take a few extra shots to capture natural moments that may happen.

5. Focus on the positives: Instead of worrying about getting the perfect shot, focus on having fun with your family. Remember that the photoshoot is a chance to create lasting memories with the people you love. If a particular shot doesn't work out, try again or move on to another shot.

User: Please provide step-by-step instructions on how to train a dog to sit and stay with clear and concise language, targeting individuals with little to no prior dog training experience. Additionally, please include tips on how to reinforce positive behavior and troubleshoot common challenges during the training process.
Assistant: Step-by-Step Instructions:

1. Start by getting the dog's attention. Say their name and make eye contact.

2. Hold a treat close to their nose, and then slowly move it upwards, causing their head to follow the treat. As their head goes up, their back end should lower down into a sit.

3. As soon as their back end hits the ground, say "sit," and give them the treat.

4. Practice this until they can sit reliably on cue.

5. To work on "stay," ask your dog to sit, and then hold your hand up, palm out, saying "stay." Start with just a few seconds and gradually increase the amount of time you ask them to stay.

6. When you release them from the stay, give them a treat and tell them "good stay."

Tips for Reinforcing Positive Behavior:

1. Use high-value treats, like small pieces of cooked chicken, to reward your dog during training sessions.

2. Be enthusiastic and use a happy tone of voice to encourage your dog.

3. Use positive reinforcement techniques to encourage good behavior, rather than punishment for bad behavior.

Troubleshooting Common Challenges:

1. If your dog appears to be ignoring you, try to increase the value of your treats or find a more exciting reward.

2. If your dog jumps up instead of sitting, try luring them into a sitting position with the treat even more slowly, so they don't have the opportunity to jump up.

3. If your dog is struggling with "stay," try releasing them after just a few seconds and gradually increasing the holding time. Additionally, you may need to work on "stay" in a quieter or less distracting environment before adding more distractions.

Assistant: Certainly! Here are some additional tips:

1. Verbal Praise: When your dog exhibits good behavior, a simple "good boy" or "good girl" can go a long way. Be sure to use an upbeat, positive tone of voice. 2. Petting: Many dogs enjoy physical touch, so a gentle stroke or pat can be an excellent way to reward good behavior. 3. Playtime: If your dog loves to play, engaging in a game of fetch or tug-of-war can be a great reward for good behavior. 4. Access to Favorite Toys: If your dog has a favorite toy, allowing them to play with it after exhibiting good behavior can be a great incentive. 5. Opportunities for Exploration: For some dogs, the opportunity to explore new environments can be a powerful reward. If your dog loves to go on walks, taking them to a new location or allowing them to sniff around in a different area can be a great reward. Remember, the most effective way to reinforce positive behavior is to use a combination of techniques, including treats, verbal praise, physical touch, playtime, and other rewards. By varying your rewards, you'll be able to keep your dog engaged and motivated during training sessions.
User: Thanks for all the tips on how to reinforce positive behavior! Do you have any advice on how to train a dog to come when called?
Assistant: Sure! Here are some tips on how to train a dog to come when called:

1. Start With Short Distances: Begin training in a quiet, distraction-free area, and start by calling your dog from a short distance away.

2. Use A Positive Tone: Use a happy, upbeat tone of voice when calling your dog. Make sure you sound excited and encouraging.

3. Reward Good Behavior: When your dog comes to you, immediately reward them with a treat, praise, or a fun game.

4. Practice Often: As your dog becomes more reliable, gradually increase the distance between you and your dog. Practice in a variety of environments with increasing distractions.

5. Avoid Punishment: Do not punish your dog if they don't come when called. This can create a negative association with being called, making it less likely that they will come in the future.

6. Use A Long Leash: For added safety during training, use a long leash while practicing recall. This will give you the ability to prevent your dog from running off if they do not respond to your recall command.

7. Make Coming Fun: Your dog should enjoy coming to you, so make sure to make it a fun experience. Run away from them, play with them, and give them plenty of praise and treats when they come to you.

Remember, each dog is different, so some dogs may take longer to learn this command than others. Be patient and keep training sessions fun and positive. With consistent training and plenty of rewards, your dog will eventually come when called every time.
User: Could you please provide some more advice on how to train a dog to stay? I'm a little worried my dog might start moving before I release him, even if I haven't said the release command yet.
Assistant: Certainly! Here are some additional tips for training your dog to stay:

1. Start Small: Begin by asking your dog to stay for just a few seconds. Gradually increase the duration of the stay as your dog becomes more reliable. 2. Use a Release Command: Choose a release command like "okay” or “free” that tells your dog they are no longer required to stay. Be consistent with using the same release command during training sessions. 3. Practice Distractions: Once your dog is comfortable with staying in a quiet environment, gradually introduce distractions. Start with low-level distractions such as toys or treats, then move up to more distracting environments such as a busy park. 4. Use Reward-Based Training: Reward your dog each time they successfully stay in place. Once your dog stays for the allotted time, use lots of praise and treats to reinforce the good behavior. 5. Monitor Body Language: Keep an eye on your dog's body language to ensure that they’re staying in place voluntarily. You can tell if your dog is uncomfortable or losing focus if they tense up, look away or move slightly. 6. Gradually Add Distance and Movement: Once your dog is consistently staying in place, start to move further away from them before returning to reward them. 7. Address Problems As They Arise: If your dog starts to move before the release command, simply return them to their original position and give the stay command again. Gradually increase the difficulty once your dog has reinforced the concept of staying in place. Remember, training takes time and patience, and dogs may take longer to learn some commands than others. Be consistent in your training, and be sure to praise and reward your dog for good behavior. With consistent effort, your dog will learn to stay in place on command.

User: Please provide step-by-step instructions on how to train a dog to sit and stay with clear and concise language, targeting individuals with little to no prior dog training experience. Assistant: Step-by-Step Instructions:

1. Start by getting the dog's attention. Say their name and make eye contact.

2. Hold a treat close to their nose, and then slowly move it upwards, causing their head to follow the treat. As their head goes up, their back end should lower down into a sit.

3. As soon as their back end hits the ground, say "sit," and give them the treat.

4. Practice this until they can sit reliably on cue.

5. To work on "stay," ask your dog to sit, and then hold your hand up, palm out, saying "stay." Start with just a few seconds and gradually increase the amount of time you ask them to stay.

6. When you release them from the stay, give them a treat and tell them "good stay."

Tips for Reinforcing Positive Behavior:

1. Use high-value treats, like small pieces of cooked chicken, to reward your dog during training sessions.

2. Be enthusiastic and use a happy tone of voice to encourage your dog.

3. Use positive reinforcement techniques to encourage good behavior, rather than punishment for bad behavior.

Troubleshooting Common Challenges:

1. If your dog appears to be ignoring you, try to increase the value of your treats or find a more exciting reward.

2. If your dog jumps up instead of sitting, try luring them into a sitting position with the treat even more slowly, so they don't have the opportunity to jump up.

3. If your dog is struggling with "stay," try releasing them after just a few seconds and gradually increasing the holding time. Additionally, you may need to work on "stay" in a quieter or less distracting environment before adding more distractions.

5. Avoid Punishment: Do not punish your dog if they don't come when called. This can create a negative association with being called, making it less likely that they will come in the future.

c31-m1.summary: The user enjoys spending time alone.
c31-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: It's nice to have someone to keep company, especially during this lockdown.
Assistant: I know, it can get pretty lonely sometimes.
User: True, but it's also an opportunity to connect more deeply with others. Like how I got to know your father better when we first met.
Assistant: Yeah, I remember you telling me how nervous you were on your first day of kindergarten. But everything turned out well.
User: Exactly! And now, I'm grateful that your father and I have each other during this time. And that woman who's staying with us, she seems to be pretty happy having someone to talk to.
Assistant: It's great that you're there for her. I'm sure she appreciates it.
User: Yes, I hope so. And who knows, maybe we'll all learn something new about each other during this time.
Assistant: I think that's a great attitude to have. We can all use this time to grow closer and learn from each other.
User: Definitely. And whenever you need someone to talk to, know that I'll always be here for you too.
Assistant: Thank you, I appreciate that. It's nice to have you as a friend as well as a parent.
User: I'm really enjoying my alone time lately. I feel like I can recharge my batteries when I'm by myself.
Assistant: That's interesting, I'm the complete opposite. I get really restless and bored when I'm alone for too long.
User: Yeah, I guess some people just thrive on being around others.
Assistant: I think it's because I'm more extroverted. Being around people gives me energy and makes me feel alive.
User: I can see how that would be the case. For me, being around people can be draining, especially if I don't have a lot in common with them.
Assistant: That makes sense. I guess we all have different needs when it comes to social interaction.
User: Definitely. It's important to know yourself and what makes you happy.
Assistant: Speaking of which, have you been able to do any of your favorite activities recently?
User: Actually, I've been spending a lot of time reading and writing. It's been really nice to have some uninterrupted time to myself.
Assistant: That sounds lovely. I've been wanting to get out into nature more. Maybe we could plan a hiking trip together sometime?
User: That sounds great! I love hiking and it would be nice to have a companion who appreciates some solitude too.

User: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: In your opinion, what are the strengths and weaknesses of Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, and would you recommend it?

Passage: Welcome to our monthly look at some of the best new tabletop games. This time around we’re solving mysteries in Victorian London, escaping from locked rooms with nothing more than brain power and playing a beautiful game from a fantasy world.
Few characters in the history of fiction can have been reimagined as often as Sherlock Holmes. Over the years he has battled nazis, confronted malevolent alien gods and even collaborated on a case with Batman.
But for my money, the most exciting take on the genre-defining investigator is Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, a tabletop mystery game first published in 1981. Now released in an updated and expanded version, it casts players as Holmes’ agents, working together to scour the streets of London and crack a succession of baffling cases.
Each game revolves around a casebook, which contains information you’ll discover as you play. You’ll start by reading an introductory scene that describes a horrible crime or impenetrable mystery, and then you’ll be let loose to investigate however you see fit. Each casebook is divided into scenes featuring different encounters, like a Choose Your Own Adventure book on steroids. You’ll visit underworld contacts in East End pubs, probe the upper echelons of Kensington society and uncover family scandals that powerful people would rather stayed hidden.
As you examine crime scenes, track down witnesses and interview suspects you’ll build a web of information, uncovering hidden motives and spotting holes in alibis. You’ll have flashes of inspiration when the disparate elements of a case suddenly slot together in your mind, and groan with frustration when it turns out you’ve been derailed by a well-placed red herring.
Eventually, when you think you can solve the case, you’ll read a final scene where Holmes explains how he arrived at the solution. You’ll win if you manage to arrive at the facts while following fewer leads than Holmes himself. As you’d expect, it’s a real challenge, but it’s also Consulting Detective’s greatest weakness, because while the game goes to incredible lengths to create a rich, bustling Victorian metropolis, it punishes players for taking the time to explore it. To win, you’ll have to be ruthlessly efficient in your investigation, which means missing out on side-scenes, supporting characters and little touches that add immensely to the feel and flavour of the game. In fact, to get the most out of each case, I’d recommend treating it less as a game than as a kind of interactive whodunnit.
There are a couple of other niggles including some anachronistic dialogue and Jack-The-Ripper-themed cases that get substantially darker than anything in the Holmes canon, which may put some players off (a previous set of cases has less disturbing subject matter). If you have any appreciation for story in games, though, this is a must-play.
Over the past couple of years, escape room games have become something of a craze. Like a cut-rate version of The Crystal Maze, they see players locked in a room and forced to solve a series of fiendish puzzles in order to get out. Many feature professionally designed sets, impressive props and even actors playing allies and antagonists for escapees to encounter on their adventures.
It can all feel like a full-scale theatrical production, but a new game aims to condense the experience into something that fits on your kitchen table. Exit: The Game traps players in one of three locations: an ancient Egyptian tomb; creepy abandoned cabin; or – as our group played – a sinister science lab. To escape, you’ll need to discover a set of hidden codes, each concealed behind a different puzzle.
Describing any of them would spoil the experience of solving them, but they revolve around decks of cards representing different locations and objects, and they rely heavily on logic, observation and lateral thinking. They are also brilliantly conceived: complex enough to be genuinely challenging, but never so difficult that they feel unfair. Collaboratively solving a tricky puzzle feels massively rewarding, and the game leads you from one challenge to the next at a pace that doesn’t get dull for a second.
Exit isn’t the only recent game to explore this theme. Unlock! Escape Adventures takes a similar approach, but works with a companion smartphone app. After playing both, though, our group unanimously agreed that while it might not be as technologically flashy, Exit had better-designed puzzles, more impressive ideas and a more satisfying progression through its succession of head-scratching mysteries. You may only be able to play each scenario once, but at £12.99, that’s pretty great value for an unforgettable evening of brain-burning fun.
It may not yet be as widely known as Game of Thrones, but author Patrick Rothfuss’ Kingkiller Chronicle is set to become the next fantasy novel series to make the jump to TV screens, with an adaptation in the works by Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda.
Rothfuss is a lifelong gamer, and in the series’ second book he introduced readers to Tak, his setting’s answer to iconic games like chess or go. In 2016, fans raised more than $1.3m (£1m) in a crowdfunding campaign to create a real-world version.
The result is a two-payer game where opponents use brown or white pieces to build a “road” – an uninterrupted path in their own colour across a square grid board. At first glance it’s reminiscent of noughts-and-crosses, Connect Four or British game show Blockbusters if you removed the need to actually answer questions. But while it’s a simple premise, there are a couple of other elements that add to Tak’s strategic challenge. Players can move pieces around the board, forming three-dimensional stacks and redistributing them in new configurations. It makes it difficult to think more than a few moves ahead, and you can also build walls, a defensive move that prevents roads being built through particular squares.
A full game of Tak in seven seconds.
Like chess or draughts, Tak takes a handful of simple rules and uses them to create genuine depth. It feels like just the kind of strategy game that could have been invented centuries ago and passed down over generations. That’s exactly as you would expect from its portrayal in the Kingkiller Chronicle, although it’s engaging enough in its own right to appeal to people who haven’t read the books. It’s awfully pricey, though, especially in the UK, where it sells for £10 more than in the US. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, I blame Brexit.
What have you been playing this month? Let us know in the comments below.

This will help you craft a more personalized message that shows you’ve done your homework. 3. Start with a compliment: Everyone appreciates a compliment, so start your conversation on a positive note. Compliment their work or a recent project they’ve completed. 4. Ask questions: Ask open-ended questions about their work or their needs. This will give you an opportunity to learn more about them and their business and show that you’re genuinely interested in what they do. 5. Follow up: If you don’t receive a reply right away, don’t be discouraged. Follow up after a week or so with a friendly reminder to keep the conversation going.

User: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: In your opinion, what are the strengths and weaknesses of Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, and would you recommend it?

Passage: Welcome to our monthly look at some of the best new tabletop games. This time around we’re solving mysteries in Victorian London, escaping from locked rooms with nothing more than brain power and playing a beautiful game from a fantasy world.
Few characters in the history of fiction can have been reimagined as often as Sherlock Holmes. Over the years he has battled nazis, confronted malevolent alien gods and even collaborated on a case with Batman.
But for my money, the most exciting take on the genre-defining investigator is Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, a tabletop mystery game first published in 1981. Now released in an updated and expanded version, it casts players as Holmes’ agents, working together to scour the streets of London and crack a succession of baffling cases.
Each game revolves around a casebook, which contains information you’ll discover as you play. You’ll start by reading an introductory scene that describes a horrible crime or impenetrable mystery, and then you’ll be let loose to investigate however you see fit. Each casebook is divided into scenes featuring different encounters, like a Choose Your Own Adventure book on steroids. You’ll visit underworld contacts in East End pubs, probe the upper echelons of Kensington society and uncover family scandals that powerful people would rather stayed hidden.
As you examine crime scenes, track down witnesses and interview suspects you’ll build a web of information, uncovering hidden motives and spotting holes in alibis. You’ll have flashes of inspiration when the disparate elements of a case suddenly slot together in your mind, and groan with frustration when it turns out you’ve been derailed by a well-placed red herring.
Eventually, when you think you can solve the case, you’ll read a final scene where Holmes explains how he arrived at the solution. You’ll win if you manage to arrive at the facts while following fewer leads than Holmes himself. As you’d expect, it’s a real challenge, but it’s also Consulting Detective’s greatest weakness, because while the game goes to incredible lengths to create a rich, bustling Victorian metropolis, it punishes players for taking the time to explore it. To win, you’ll have to be ruthlessly efficient in your investigation, which means missing out on side-scenes, supporting characters and little touches that add immensely to the feel and flavour of the game. In fact, to get the most out of each case, I’d recommend treating it less as a game than as a kind of interactive whodunnit.
There are a couple of other niggles including some anachronistic dialogue and Jack-The-Ripper-themed cases that get substantially darker than anything in the Holmes canon, which may put some players off (a previous set of cases has less disturbing subject matter). If you have any appreciation for story in games, though, this is a must-play.
Over the past couple of years, escape room games have become something of a craze. Like a cut-rate version of The Crystal Maze, they see players locked in a room and forced to solve a series of fiendish puzzles in order to get out. Many feature professionally designed sets, impressive props and even actors playing allies and antagonists for escapees to encounter on their adventures.
It can all feel like a full-scale theatrical production, but a new game aims to condense the experience into something that fits on your kitchen table. Exit: The Game traps players in one of three locations: an ancient Egyptian tomb; creepy abandoned cabin; or – as our group played – a sinister science lab. To escape, you’ll need to discover a set of hidden codes, each concealed behind a different puzzle.
Describing any of them would spoil the experience of solving them, but they revolve around decks of cards representing different locations and objects, and they rely heavily on logic, observation and lateral thinking. They are also brilliantly conceived: complex enough to be genuinely challenging, but never so difficult that they feel unfair. Collaboratively solving a tricky puzzle feels massively rewarding, and the game leads you from one challenge to the next at a pace that doesn’t get dull for a second.
Exit isn’t the only recent game to explore this theme. Unlock! Escape Adventures takes a similar approach, but works with a companion smartphone app. After playing both, though, our group unanimously agreed that while it might not be as technologically flashy, Exit had better-designed puzzles, more impressive ideas and a more satisfying progression through its succession of head-scratching mysteries. You may only be able to play each scenario once, but at £12.99, that’s pretty great value for an unforgettable evening of brain-burning fun.
It may not yet be as widely known as Game of Thrones, but author Patrick Rothfuss’ Kingkiller Chronicle is set to become the next fantasy novel series to make the jump to TV screens, with an adaptation in the works by Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda.
Rothfuss is a lifelong gamer, and in the series’ second book he introduced readers to Tak, his setting’s answer to iconic games like chess or go. In 2016, fans raised more than $1.3m (£1m) in a crowdfunding campaign to create a real-world version.
The result is a two-payer game where opponents use brown or white pieces to build a “road” – an uninterrupted path in their own colour across a square grid board. At first glance it’s reminiscent of noughts-and-crosses, Connect Four or British game show Blockbusters if you removed the need to actually answer questions. But while it’s a simple premise, there are a couple of other elements that add to Tak’s strategic challenge. Players can move pieces around the board, forming three-dimensional stacks and redistributing them in new configurations. It makes it difficult to think more than a few moves ahead, and you can also build walls, a defensive move that prevents roads being built through particular squares.
A full game of Tak in seven seconds.
Like chess or draughts, Tak takes a handful of simple rules and uses them to create genuine depth. It feels like just the kind of strategy game that could have been invented centuries ago and passed down over generations. That’s exactly as you would expect from its portrayal in the Kingkiller Chronicle, although it’s engaging enough in its own right to appeal to people who haven’t read the books. It’s awfully pricey, though, especially in the UK, where it sells for £10 more than in the US. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, I blame Brexit.

User: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: In your opinion, what are the strengths and weaknesses of Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, and would you recommend it?

Passage: Welcome to our monthly look at some of the best new tabletop games. This time around we’re solving mysteries in Victorian London, escaping from locked rooms with nothing more than brain power and playing a beautiful game from a fantasy world.
Few characters in the history of fiction can have been reimagined as often as Sherlock Holmes. Over the years he has battled nazis, confronted malevolent alien gods and even collaborated on a case with Batman.
But for my money, the most exciting take on the genre-defining investigator is Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, a tabletop mystery game first published in 1981. Now released in an updated and expanded version, it casts players as Holmes’ agents, working together to scour the streets of London and crack a succession of baffling cases.
Each game revolves around a casebook, which contains information you’ll discover as you play. You’ll start by reading an introductory scene that describes a horrible crime or impenetrable mystery, and then you’ll be let loose to investigate however you see fit. Each casebook is divided into scenes featuring different encounters, like a Choose Your Own Adventure book on steroids. You’ll visit underworld contacts in East End pubs, probe the upper echelons of Kensington society and uncover family scandals that powerful people would rather stayed hidden.
As you examine crime scenes, track down witnesses and interview suspects you’ll build a web of information, uncovering hidden motives and spotting holes in alibis. You’ll have flashes of inspiration when the disparate elements of a case suddenly slot together in your mind, and groan with frustration when it turns out you’ve been derailed by a well-placed red herring.
Eventually, when you think you can solve the case, you’ll read a final scene where Holmes explains how he arrived at the solution. You’ll win if you manage to arrive at the facts while following fewer leads than Holmes himself. As you’d expect, it’s a real challenge, but it’s also Consulting Detective’s greatest weakness, because while the game goes to incredible lengths to create a rich, bustling Victorian metropolis, it punishes players for taking the time to explore it. To win, you’ll have to be ruthlessly efficient in your investigation, which means missing out on side-scenes, supporting characters and little touches that add immensely to the feel and flavour of the game. In fact, to get the most out of each case, I’d recommend treating it less as a game than as a kind of interactive whodunnit.
There are a couple of other niggles including some anachronistic dialogue and Jack-The-Ripper-themed cases that get substantially darker than anything in the Holmes canon, which may put some players off (a previous set of cases has less disturbing subject matter). If you have any appreciation for story in games, though, this is a must-play.
Over the past couple of years, escape room games have become something of a craze. Like a cut-rate version of The Crystal Maze, they see players locked in a room and forced to solve a series of fiendish puzzles in order to get out. Many feature professionally designed sets, impressive props and even actors playing allies and antagonists for escapees to encounter on their adventures.
It can all feel like a full-scale theatrical production, but a new game aims to condense the experience into something that fits on your kitchen table. Exit: The Game traps players in one of three locations: an ancient Egyptian tomb; creepy abandoned cabin; or – as our group played – a sinister science lab. To escape, you’ll need to discover a set of hidden codes, each concealed behind a different puzzle.
Describing any of them would spoil the experience of solving them, but they revolve around decks of cards representing different locations and objects, and they rely heavily on logic, observation and lateral thinking. They are also brilliantly conceived: complex enough to be genuinely challenging, but never so difficult that they feel unfair. Collaboratively solving a tricky puzzle feels massively rewarding, and the game leads you from one challenge to the next at a pace that doesn’t get dull for a second.
Exit isn’t the only recent game to explore this theme. Unlock! Escape Adventures takes a similar approach, but works with a companion smartphone app. After playing both, though, our group unanimously agreed that while it might not be as technologically flashy, Exit had better-designed puzzles, more impressive ideas and a more satisfying progression through its succession of head-scratching mysteries. You may only be able to play each scenario once, but at £12.99, that’s pretty great value for an unforgettable evening of brain-burning fun.
It may not yet be as widely known as Game of Thrones, but author Patrick Rothfuss’ Kingkiller Chronicle is set to become the next fantasy novel series to make the jump to TV screens, with an adaptation in the works by Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda.
Rothfuss is a lifelong gamer, and in the series’ second book he introduced readers to Tak, his setting’s answer to iconic games like chess or go. In 2016, fans raised more than $1.3m (£1m) in a crowdfunding campaign to create a real-world version.
The result is a two-payer game where opponents use brown or white pieces to build a “road” – an uninterrupted path in their own colour across a square grid board. At first glance it’s reminiscent of noughts-and-crosses, Connect Four or British game show Blockbusters if you removed the need to actually answer questions. But while it’s a simple premise, there are a couple of other elements that add to Tak’s strategic challenge. Players can move pieces around the board, forming three-dimensional stacks and redistributing them in new configurations. It makes it difficult to think more than a few moves ahead, and you can also build walls, a defensive move that prevents roads being built through particular squares.
A full game of Tak in seven seconds.
Like chess or draughts, Tak takes a handful of simple rules and uses them to create genuine depth. It feels like just the kind of strategy game that could have been invented centuries ago and passed down over generations. That’s exactly as you would expect from its portrayal in the Kingkiller Chronicle, although it’s engaging enough in its own right to appeal to people who haven’t read the books. It’s awfully pricey, though, especially in the UK, where it sells for £10 more than in the US. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, I blame Brexit.

As you examine crime scenes, track down witnesses and interview suspects you’ll build a web of information, uncovering hidden motives and spotting holes in alibis. You’ll have flashes of inspiration when the disparate elements of a case suddenly slot together in your mind, and groan with frustration when it turns out you’ve been derailed by a well-placed red herring.
Eventually, when you think you can solve the case, you’ll read a final scene where Holmes explains how he arrived at the solution. You’ll win if you manage to arrive at the facts while following fewer leads than Holmes himself. As you’d expect, it’s a real challenge, but it’s also Consulting Detective’s greatest weakness, because while the game goes to incredible lengths to create a rich, bustling Victorian metropolis, it punishes players for taking the time to explore it. To win, you’ll have to be ruthlessly efficient in your investigation, which means missing out on side-scenes, supporting characters and little touches that add immensely to the feel and flavour of the game. In fact, to get the most out of each case, I’d recommend treating it less as a game than as a kind of interactive whodunnit.
There are a couple of other niggles including some anachronistic dialogue and Jack-The-Ripper-themed cases that get substantially darker than anything in the Holmes canon, which may put some players off (a previous set of cases has less disturbing subject matter). If you have any appreciation for story in games, though, this is a must-play.
Over the past couple of years, escape room games have become something of a craze. Like a cut-rate version of The Crystal Maze, they see players locked in a room and forced to solve a series of fiendish puzzles in order to get out. Many feature professionally designed sets, impressive props and even actors playing allies and antagonists for escapees to encounter on their adventures.
It can all feel like a full-scale theatrical production, but a new game aims to condense the experience into something that fits on your kitchen table. Exit: The Game traps players in one of three locations: an ancient Egyptian tomb; creepy abandoned cabin; or – as our group played – a sinister science lab. To escape, you’ll need to discover a set of hidden codes, each concealed behind a different puzzle.
Describing any of them would spoil the experience of solving them, but they revolve around decks of cards representing different locations and objects, and they rely heavily on logic, observation and lateral thinking. They are also brilliantly conceived: complex enough to be genuinely challenging, but never so difficult that they feel unfair. Collaboratively solving a tricky puzzle feels massively rewarding, and the game leads you from one challenge to the next at a pace that doesn’t get dull for a second.
Exit isn’t the only recent game to explore this theme. Unlock! Escape Adventures takes a similar approach, but works with a companion smartphone app. After playing both, though, our group unanimously agreed that while it might not be as technologically flashy, Exit had better-designed puzzles, more impressive ideas and a more satisfying progression through its succession of head-scratching mysteries. You may only be able to play each scenario once, but at £12.99, that’s pretty great value for an unforgettable evening of brain-burning fun.
It may not yet be as widely known as Game of Thrones, but author Patrick Rothfuss’ Kingkiller Chronicle is set to become the next fantasy novel series to make the jump to TV screens, with an adaptation in the works by Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda.
Rothfuss is a lifelong gamer, and in the series’ second book he introduced readers to Tak, his setting’s answer to iconic games like chess or go. In 2016, fans raised more than $1.3m (£1m) in a crowdfunding campaign to create a real-world version.
The result is a two-payer game where opponents use brown or white pieces to build a “road” – an uninterrupted path in their own colour across a square grid board. At first glance it’s reminiscent of noughts-and-crosses, Connect Four or British game show Blockbusters if you removed the need to actually answer questions. But while it’s a simple premise, there are a couple of other elements that add to Tak’s strategic challenge. Players can move pieces around the board, forming three-dimensional stacks and redistributing them in new configurations. It makes it difficult to think more than a few moves ahead, and you can also build walls, a defensive move that prevents roads being built through particular squares.
A full game of Tak in seven seconds.
Like chess or draughts, Tak takes a handful of simple rules and uses them to create genuine depth. It feels like just the kind of strategy game that could have been invented centuries ago and passed down over generations. That’s exactly as you would expect from its portrayal in the Kingkiller Chronicle, although it’s engaging enough in its own right to appeal to people who haven’t read the books. It’s awfully pricey, though, especially in the UK, where it sells for £10 more than in the US. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, I blame Brexit.
